title: Pascal’s Wager — belief as a decision under uncertainty
when: Pascal drafted the fragment during the final years of his life (1656–1662; its exact date is uncertain). His unfinished notes were published posthumously in the 1670 Pensées.
people: Blaise Pascal; later decision theorists and philosophers of religion.
origin: Seventeenth-century French Catholic thought, within Pascal’s effort to assemble an unfinished defense of Christianity and his mathematical study of games of chance.
idea: Pascal asks a skeptic to treat belief in God as an unavoidable wager. In the familiar argument, if God exists, belief may bring infinite happiness; if not, the loss is finite. If the chance of God’s existence is positive, the potentially infinite payoff appears to favor wagering for God. This is a prudential argument about what to do under uncertainty, not evidence that God exists. Pascal also recognizes that belief may not be chosen at will and suggests religious practice as a route toward it. The fragment’s intended role—and whether Pascal meant it to convert unbelievers—remains contested.
relevance: The wager separates reasons for believing something is true from the stakes of acting as though it might be true. Its critics ask whether infinite outcomes break ordinary expected-utility calculations, whether belief can be voluntary, and how the argument handles rival religions. It remains a sharp test case in decision theory and philosophy of religion, not a settled proof.
